reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: The most common cause of peripheral vertigo, characterised by brief spinning episodes triggered by changes in head position
Typical triggers include rolling over in bed, lying down, looking up or bending forward
Each episode is short-lived, usually lasting seconds to under a minute, and there is no associated hearing loss or tinnitus
The posterior semicircular canal is most often involved because of its dependent position
The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces symptoms and elicits characteristic positional nystagmus with a brief latency and fatigability
Management principles rely on canalith repositioning manoeuvres such as the Epley manoeuvre rather than long-term drug therapy
Vestibular sedatives are generally unhelpful and may hinder central compensation if used long term
Recurrences are common but usually respond again to repositioning; atypical or persistent features should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by displacement of otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) from the utricular macula into a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal. In the common canalithiasis form, these free-floating particles move under gravity when the head changes position, creating abnormal endolymph flow that deflects the cupula and generates a transient, mismatched sensation of rotation. The brief latency, short duration and fatigability of symptoms reflect the settling of the particles. A less common cupulolithiasis form, with particles adherent to the cupula, produces more persistent positional nystagmus.
additionalDifferentials: Central positional vertigo from posterior fossa pathology
additionalInvestigations: Dix-Hallpike test for posterior canal involvement
Supine roll (head-turn) test for suspected horizontal canal disease
Otoscopy and hearing assessment to exclude other otological causes
Neurological examination to exclude central causes
Imaging of the brain and posterior fossa only if central pathology is suspected
redFlags: Atypical nystagmus that is purely vertical, direction-changing or non-fatiguing suggesting a central cause
Associated neurological signs, severe headache or gait ataxia
Accompanying hearing loss or tinnitus pointing to alternative inner ear disease
Persistent continuous vertigo rather than brief positional episodes
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and often self-limiting, with excellent response to repositioning manoeuvres, although recurrences over time are common and occasionally require repeat treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking central positional vertigo for BPPV and missing serious pathology
Relying on vestibular suppressant drugs instead of repositioning manoeuvres
Failing to identify the affected canal, leading to ineffective treatment
Overlooking coexisting hearing loss that indicates a different diagnosis
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Canalith repositioning manoeuvres, principally the Epley manoeuvre, for the common posterior canal disease
Barbecue (Lempert) roll or Gufoni manoeuvre for horizontal semicircular canal involvement
Teaching patient-performed home repositioning exercises to reinforce treatment and manage recurrence
Reassurance about the benign, often self-limiting course, avoiding long-term vestibular sedatives that hinder central compensation
Short-term antiemetics reserved only for acute severe nausea rather than as ongoing therapy
Reassessment with a repeat Dix-Hallpike test to confirm resolution and detect recurrence
Referral to ENT or neurology for atypical, refractory or central features
